qs.q: Find the average of 102, 107, 99, 104, 98.
qs.h: §1, deviation method — take A = 100 and average the deviations.
qs.s: Take A = 100. Deviations: +2, +7, −1, +4, −2, summing to 10. Average = 100 + 10/5 = 102.

qs.q: The average of 5 numbers is 27. Each number is increased by 4 and the result is then doubled. The new average is
qs.h: §2, the two transformation properties. Apply them in the stated order.
qs.s: Adding 4 raises the average to 31; doubling then doubles it to 62.

qs.q: The average of 11 consecutive integers is 17. Find the largest of them.
qs.h: §2, last bullet — for an AP the average is the middle term.
qs.s: For 11 consecutive integers the average is the 6th (middle) term, so the middle is 17. The numbers run 12 to 22; largest = 22.

qs.q: The average of five distinct positive integers is 10. What is the largest possible value of any one of them?
qs.h: §1, Sum = Average × Count. To push one value up, make the other four as small as they are allowed to be — and note "distinct".
qs.s: Total = 5 × 10 = 50. To maximise one value, minimise the other four distinct positive integers: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Largest = 50 − 10 = 40.

qs.q: The average of 20 numbers is 45. If the average of the first 12 of them is 42, the average of the remaining 8 is
qs.h: §13, the two-line method — convert both averages to sums, subtract, divide once.
qs.s: Total = 900. First twelve sum to 504, so the rest sum to 396. Average = 396/8 = 49.5.

qs.q: In a class, 30 boys average 55 marks and 20 girls average 70 marks. Find the class average.
qs.h: §3, the central formula. Then run the §3 sanity check — the answer must lie closer to 55.
qs.s: (30 × 55 + 20 × 70)/50 = (1650 + 1400)/50 = 61. Check: 61 is nearer 55 than 70, and boys are the larger group ✓.

qs.q: A shopkeeper sells 40 kg of rice at ₹25/kg and 60 kg at ₹35/kg. The average selling price per kg is
qs.h: §3 — the two quantities are unequal, so a plain mean of 25 and 35 is wrong.

qs.q: In a class of 60 students, boys average 62 marks and girls average 74 marks, while the class averages 71. Find the number of boys.
qs.h: §4, the backward direction — use alligation to get the boys : girls ratio first.
qs.s: Alligation about 71: boys : girls = (74 − 71) : (71 − 62) = 3 : 9 = 1 : 3. Of 60 students, boys = 60 × 1/4 = 15.

qs.q: In a company, 40% of the employees are women. Men average ₹50,000 and women average ₹60,000 per month. The company average is
qs.h: §3 — the percentages are the weights. You do not need the actual head count.

qs.q: Sections A, B and C have 25, 35 and 40 students averaging 70, 65 and 60 marks respectively. Find the overall average.
qs.h: §3 extended to three groups, or §13's master relation Total = Σ(size × average).

qs.q: The average weight of 10 people increases by 1.5 kg when a new person replaces one weighing 58 kg. Find the weight (in kg) of the new person.
qs.h: §5, the general rule — new value = old value + (n × change in average).
qs.s: Total increase = 10 × 1.5 = 15 kg. New person = 58 + 15 = 73.

qs.q: The average of 12 numbers is 25. When one number is removed, the average of the rest is 24. The removed number is
qs.h: §5 — work with totals: 12 × 25 minus 11 × 24.

qs.q: The average age of 15 students is 14 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average becomes 15 years. Find the teacher's age.
qs.h: §5, the adding variant — new member's value = (n+1)A′ − nA. It is not 15.
qs.s: 16 × 15 − 15 × 14 = 240 − 210 = 30. (Not 15 — the teacher must also pull the other fifteen up.)

qs.q: The average score of 11 players is 32. The captain, who scored 50, leaves and a new player joins; the average becomes 31. The new player's score is
qs.h: §5 — total before, total after, and the 50 that left. Three sums, one subtraction.
qs.s: Original total = 352. After the swap the total is 11 × 31 = 341. Without the captain the other ten total 352 − 50 = 302, so the new player scored 341 − 302 = 39.

qs.q: In a group of 8 people, two members weighing 55 kg and 60 kg are replaced by two new members, and the average weight rises by 3 kg. Find the combined weight (in kg) of the two new members.
qs.h: §5 — the total change is still n × (change in average), regardless of how many members were swapped.
qs.s: Total increase = 8 × 3 = 24 kg. Combined new weight = (55 + 60) + 24 = 139.

qs.q: The average of 25 numbers was computed as 40, but one number was read as 36 instead of 63. Find the correct average.
qs.h: §6 — adjust the sum by the error first, then divide once.
qs.s: The sum was understated by 63 − 36 = 27. Correct average = 40 + 27/25 = 40 + 1.08 = 41.08.

qs.q: The average of 10 numbers is 62. It is later found that 85 was read as 58, and 45 was read as 54. Find the correct average.
qs.h: §6 — the two errors go in opposite directions. Compute the net correction to the sum.

qs.q: The average marks of 50 students was found to be 72. It was then discovered that two students' marks were entered as 48 and 55 instead of the correct 84 and 45. The correct average is
qs.h: §6 — net error = (84 − 48) + (45 − 55). Watch the sign of the second one.

qs.q: A car travels from A to B at 30 km/h and returns at 70 km/h. Find the average speed (in km/h) for the whole journey.
qs.h: §7, equal distances ⟹ harmonic mean 2ab/(a+b). It is not 50.

qs.q: A man cycles at 12 km/h for 3 hours and then at 18 km/h for 3 hours. His average speed is
qs.h: §7 — read for whether time or distance is equal. Here it is time.
qs.s: Equal times ⟹ plain average (12 + 18)/2 = 15.

qs.q: A man covers three equal stretches of a road at 20 km/h, 30 km/h and 60 km/h. Find his average speed (in km/h).
qs.h: §7, last line — average = 3/(1/a + 1/b + 1/c).

qs.q: A person travels 60 km at 30 km/h and the next 90 km at 45 km/h. Find the average speed (in km/h).
qs.h: §7, the definition — total distance / total time. The distances are unequal, so no shortcut formula applies.
qs.s: Times: 60/30 = 2 h and 90/45 = 2 h, so 4 h for 150 km ⟹ 37.5 km/h.

qs.q: The AM of two positive numbers is 10 and their GM is 8. Their HM is
qs.h: §8 — GM² = AM × HM.

qs.q: Two positive numbers have a sum of 30. Find their maximum possible product.
qs.h: §8, general principle — for a fixed sum the product is maximised when the terms are equal.
qs.s: Product is maximal at equality: 15 × 15 = 225.

qs.q: The AM of two positive numbers is 13 and their GM is 12. Find the positive difference between the two numbers.
qs.h: §8 with §1 of `13-Algebra.md` — (a − b)² = (a + b)² − 4ab.
qs.s: a + b = 26 and ab = 144. (a − b)² = 676 − 576 = 100 ⟹ difference = 10. (The numbers are 18 and 8.)

qs.q: A quantity grows by 25% in the first year and by 80% in the second. The average annual growth rate is
qs.h: §9 — the quantities multiply, so take the geometric mean of the growth factors, not the arithmetic mean of the rates.
qs.s: Factors 1.25 and 1.80 multiply to 2.25; √2.25 = 1.5 ⟹ 50% per year. (The arithmetic mean, 52.5%, is the trap.)

qs.q: For positive reals a and b, find the minimum value of (a + b)(1/a + 1/b).
qs.h: §8 — expand first; you will be left with 2 + (a/b + b/a), and x + 1/x ≥ 2.
qs.s: Expand: (a + b)(1/a + 1/b) = 2 + a/b + b/a ≥ 2 + 2 = 4, with equality at a = b.

qs.q: Find the average of the first 75 natural numbers.
qs.h: §10, first bullet — (n+1)/2.

qs.q: The average of the first 20 odd natural numbers is
qs.h: §10 — the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².
qs.s: Sum of the first 20 odd numbers = 20² = 400; average = 400/20 = 20.

qs.q: The average of the first n even natural numbers is 31. Find n.
qs.h: §10 — the average of the first n even numbers is n + 1.
qs.s: Average of the first n even numbers = n + 1 = 31 ⟹ n = 30.

qs.q: For the data set 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 100, the median is
qs.h: §11 — with an even count the median is the average of the two middle terms. One option is the mean, which the outlier has dragged upward.
qs.s: Sorted, the two middle terms are 7 and 9 ⟹ median = 8. The mean, 140/6 ≈ 23.33, is dragged up by the outlier 100.

qs.q: A class of 50 students averages 60 marks. A sub-group of 20 averages 45. Find the average of the remaining 30.
qs.h: §13, third worked example — totals, subtract, divide once.
qs.s: Total = 3000; sub-group total = 900 ⟹ remainder = 2100 over 30 = 70.

qs.q: The average age of a group is 25 years. When 6 people of average age 32 join, the group's average becomes 27. Find the original number of people.
qs.h: §12, the alligation shortcut — get original : new as a ratio, then scale using the 6.
qs.s: Alligation about 27: original : new = (32 − 27) : (27 − 25) = 5 : 2. New = 6 ⟹ original = 15. (Check: (375 + 192)/21 = 27 ✓.)

qs.q: A class averages 72 marks. The 15 girls average 80 and the boys average 66. The number of boys is
qs.h: §13, missing sub-group size — alligation gives boys : girls directly.
qs.s: Alligation about 72: boys : girls = (80 − 72) : (72 − 66) = 8 : 6 = 4 : 3. Girls = 15 ⟹ boys = 20.

qs.q: Of five numbers, the average of the first three is 14 and the average of the last three is 18. If the third number is 16, find the average of all five.
qs.h: §13, the nested-group version — the two stated groups overlap in the third number, so subtract it once.
qs.s: First three sum to 42, last three to 54; total 96 counts the third number twice. Sum of all five = 96 − 16 = 80 ⟹ average = 16.

qs.q: A firm has three departments. Department A has 12 people averaging ₹30,000; department B has 18 people averaging ₹45,000. All 40 employees average ₹42,000. Find department C's average salary (in ₹).
qs.h: §13, master relation — Total = Σ(size × average). First work out how many people are in C.
qs.s: Total = 40 × 42 = 1680 (thousands). A + B = 360 + 810 = 1170. C has 40 − 30 = 10 people totalling 510 ⟹ average ₹51,000.

qs.q: The average of 7 numbers is 40. The average of the first four is 35 and the average of the last four is 47. The fourth number is
qs.h: §13 — the two groups of four overlap in exactly one number.
qs.s: First four sum to 140, last four to 188; total 328 counts the fourth number twice. All seven sum to 280 ⟹ fourth = 328 − 280 = 48.

qs.q: A group of 60 students averages 55 marks. The boys average 50 and the girls average 65. The number of girls is
qs.h: Alligation about 55.
qs.s: Alligation about 55: boys : girls = (65 − 55) : (55 − 50) = 2 : 1 ⟹ girls = 60 × 1/3 = 20.

qs.q: A cyclist covers 40 km at 40 km/h and the next 40 km at 60 km/h. Find the average speed (in km/h).
qs.h: Equal distances ⟹ harmonic mean.
qs.s: Equal distances ⟹ 2(40)(60)/100 = 48.

qs.q: The average of 15 numbers is 18. If 3 is added to each number and the result is then multiplied by 2, the new average is
qs.h: Apply the transformations in order.
qs.s: Adding 3 gives 21; doubling gives 42.

qs.q: The average weight of 6 people is 68 kg. One person weighing 75 kg leaves. Find the average weight (in kg) of the remaining five.
qs.h: Totals.
qs.s: Total = 408; after the person leaves, 333 over 5 = 66.6.

qs.q: The AM of two positive numbers is 15 and their HM is 9.6. Their GM is
qs.h: GM² = AM × HM.

qs.q: The average of 11 results is 50. The average of the first six is 49 and the average of the last six is 52. Find the sixth result.
qs.h: The two groups of six overlap in the sixth result.
qs.s: First six sum to 294, last six to 312; total 606 counts the sixth twice. All eleven sum to 550 ⟹ sixth = 606 − 550 = 56.

qs.q: The average of 30 numbers was computed as 24. Two numbers had been read as 15 and 32 instead of the correct 51 and 23. The correct average is
qs.h: Net error, then divide once.

qs.q: The average age of a family of 5 members is 20 years. The youngest member is 10 years old. What was the average age (in years) of the family at the time the youngest member was born?
qs.h: Only the other four existed then — and each was 10 years younger.
qs.s: Current total = 100, so the other four members total 90 now. Ten years ago they totalled 90 − 40 = 50, giving an average of 12.5 for the family that existed then.
